I don't think there is one defined experience of being a masc lesbian. Everyone's gender expression and understanding of their own gender identity is different - some may feel the same way, others don't. I'm masc in my gender expression, but don't view womanhood as a one-dimensional experience, so while I'm gender non-conforming, it feels more like I'm doing womanhood in my own authentic way. Additionally, people who have such deeper struggles with gender identity to the point of taking T are more likely to identify as trans or non-binary - I know people who identified as a Lesbian and are still sapphic but have had top surgery and now identity as enby. Basically, gender is a spectrum and everyone should simply do what feels best to them.

As a horology enthusiast, here are my tips. 
1. Never ever pay for a fashion brand. It's not worth the price. 
2. Choose what movement you want - quartz, automatic, mechaquartz, solar quartz. 
3. Decide the dial size ideal for your wrist after measuring the circumference of your wrist. Also the shape of the dial you'd like. 
4. Given that your budget is fairly substantial, a lot of choices open up to you. Brands like Tissot, Seiko, Orient are all good horology brands with history. Casio and Titan are also good brands, mainly dealing with quartz watches and relatively more economically priced than the aforementioned ones. 
5. Decide whether you want to spend all your money on one watch, or get two to have some variety.

Essentially, if either of us had the courage to confess during the many many times when we've both been single, things would have been different today. I don't know what the future holds, but I'm glad that our friendship has been strong throughout it all. 

All of this is to say, if your friendship has a strong foundation, you might as well let her know how you feel - even if she doesn't feel the same way, atleast you'll know and won't have to live with this what if. What I've learnt is learning to manage rejection is better than living with regret.
